case.subject: Incident review
case.title: Payment API outage postmortem and actions

canvasName: R1-C07 Payment API outage postmortem and actions

segments.text: This is the postmortem for the payment API outage on Tuesday. The incident lasted fifty two minutes, from 14:07 to 14:59 UTC. During that window, about sixty percent of card payments failed, and some customers saw a generic error page. No money was lost, but we violated our error budget for the quarter and we need to understand both the technical cause and the process gaps. This meeting is blameless.
segments.textReply: Added the incident summary: a 52-minute outage, approximately 60% of card payments failing, generic error pages for some customers, and no money lost. The review is marked blameless; technical causes and process gaps remain to investigate.

segments.text: We are here to find system problems, not to assign personal fault. Let's build the timeline. At 13:55, we deployed release 4.18.2, which included a small change to the connection pool settings. At 14:03, the first alert fired for elevated latency on the payment service. At 14:07, error rate crossed five percent. The on call engineer acknowledged at 14:09 and began checking dashboards.

segments.text: At 14:14, the team saw database connection timeouts. At 14:21, they rolled back the release, but the error rate did not recover. At 14:32, they discovered that the DNS resolver was returning a stale address for one of the primary database replicas. At 14:41, they failed over to the secondary replica and traffic recovered. At 14:59, error rate returned to baseline and the incident was closed.
segments.textReply: Added the database timeouts, rollback, stale DNS discovery, and failover recovery to the timeline.

segments.text: The direct cause was a combination of two changes. The release reduced the connection pool timeout from five seconds to two seconds, which made the service less tolerant of slow DNS. Separately, a network change on Monday had reduced the DNS cache TTL, so the resolver was more likely to return stale records during a failover. The stale record pointed to a replica that had been taken out of service.
segments.textReply: I’m adding the two interacting changes and showing how stale DNS led to the unavailable replica.

segments.text: The service kept retrying the stale address, and the shortened timeout turned a slowdown into a hard failure. Why did the rollback not fix it? Because the DNS record was already cached, and the rollback did not flush the resolver cache. The team assumed the release was the only change. The runbook said to roll back first, then check dependencies, but it did not say to verify DNS after a rollback.
segments.textReply: Added the retry/timeout interaction, why rollback didn’t clear the cached DNS record, and the runbook’s missing DNS verification step.

segments.text: That is a process gap. The on call had the authority to fail over, but they waited for the database team because the runbook described failover as a last resort. That added about nine minutes. Detection was also slower than it should have been. The latency alert fired at 14:03, but it was a warning, not a page. The error rate alert paged at 14:07. We had no synthetic check for card payments from an external region.
segments.textReply: Added the process and detection gaps: failover approval added about nine minutes, the latency alert was warning-only, and no external-region synthetic payment check existed.

segments.text: The dashboard showed service level error rate, but not the percentage of payment attempts that never reached the service. If we had a synthetic payment probe, we might have caught the failure at 14:05. Customer impact. About eighteen thousand payment attempts failed. Most were retried successfully within ten minutes. Four hundred customers saw a duplicate authorization hold, which we reversed automatically by 16:30.
segments.textReply: Added the impact details: about 18,000 failed attempts, most recovered on retry within ten minutes, and 400 duplicate authorization holds reversed by 16:30. Also noted that the dashboard missed attempts that never reached the service and a synthetic probe might have detected the issue at 14:05.

segments.text: Support received two hundred and ten tickets. The status page was updated at 14:26, nineteen minutes after the incident started. That is too slow. We need a template and a designated communications owner. Now the contributing factors. First, the config change was not covered by a canary in the payment path. Second, the DNS dependency was not in the service map.
segments.textReply: Added the support and communications gap—210 tickets and a status update 19 minutes after onset—and the two contributing factors: no payment-path canary and a missing DNS dependency in the service map.

segments.text: Third, the runbook did not include cache invalidation or DNS verification. Fourth, the failover decision required a second team, which added latency. Fifth, the status page update was manual and owned by whoever was on call. Sixth, the alert thresholds were tuned for a single region, not for the payment path as a whole. The action items need owners and dates.

Third, change the connection pool timeout back to five seconds and add a canary that runs for thirty minutes before full rollout.

shapes.title: Post-meeting summary · Payment API outage
shapes.html:
Payment API outage — blameless review
Purpose: understand the system and process conditions behind Tuesday’s 52-minute outage, agree corrective actions, and protect payment reliability.
Impact
~60% of card payments failed; ~18,000 attempts failed. Most succeeded on retry within 10 minutes. 400 duplicate holds were reversed by 16:30. No money lost.
Incident
14:07–14:59 UTC · 52 minutes
Sev 1 · quarterly error budget exhausted

Key decisions

  • Keep the incident-channel structure and automatic duplicate-hold reversal; retain clean rollback and incident communication practices.
  • On-call gets explicit authority to fail over databases; update escalation policy. Add DNS verification and resolver-cache checks to operations and release workflows.
  • Run a five-minute pre-deploy DNS and DB health check; require a 30-minute canary for timeout, connection-pool, or retry changes.
  • Assign a single incident commander for every Sev 1 and target the first status-page update within 15 minutes; introduce a template and communications rotation.
  • Review actions weekly until closed. Payment-path feature changes require reliability review while the quarterly error budget is exhausted. This is policy, not punishment.
  • Hold a follow-up review in two weeks; owners should flag date risks before Friday.

Action items

Open risks & follow-up

  • Stale DNS can persist across rollback unless resolver cache handling is explicit; DNS dependency was absent from the service map.
  • Existing service-level error rate missed payment attempts that never reached the service. Synthetic, external-region, payment-path coverage is needed; single-region alert thresholds were insufficient.
  • Failover coordination added about nine minutes; status updates were manual and ownership unclear. Track the new authority, incident commander, and communications process.
  • Follow-up in two weeks: verify synthetic probe, runbook, canary, and status-page template. Review all actions weekly until closed; raise schedule risks before Friday.

Incident timeline · UTC

13:55 Release 4.18.214:03 Latency warning14:07 Errors >5%; outage starts14:09 On-call acknowledges14:14 DB timeouts14:21 Rollback; errors persist14:32 Stale replica DNS found14:41 Failover; recovery14:59 Baseline restored; closed
Blameless framing: the release timeout reduction (5s to 2s) and Monday’s DNS cache TTL change interacted; retries hit a stale address for a retired replica. Cached DNS survived rollback, and the runbook omitted DNS verification.
